subject: ophthalmology
title: Anterior uveitis

steps.tx: **Acute anterior uveitis** presents with a red painful eye with photophobia, circumcorneal congestion, cells and flare in the anterior chamber, deposits on the corneal endothelium called keratic precipitates, a small pupil and altered pressure. **Granulomatous** inflammation produces large mutton fat precipitates with iris nodules at the pupil margin called Koeppe nodules and in the stroma called Busacca nodules. **Nongranulomatous** attacks linked with HLA-B27 produce fine precipitates with fibrin and sometimes hypopyon. Slit lamp grading of cells and flare guides severity and response.
steps.say: An acute anterior uveitis attack produces a red painful eye that fears light and waters constantly. The slit lamp shows cells and flare floating in the front chamber with deposits sitting on the corneal endothelium. Large greasy mutton fat deposits with iris nodules point toward granulomatous disease such as sarcoidosis or tuberculosis. Fine deposits with fibrin and a fluid level of pus point toward HLA-B27 linked nongranulomatous disease.

vis.alt: Slit lamp view showing circumcorneal injection, anterior chamber cells and flare, fine and mutton fat keratic precipitates, and iris nodules (Koeppe, Busacca) characteristic of anterior uveitis.
vis.caption: Key clinical signs of acute anterior uveitis, distinguishing granulomatous and non-granulomatous forms. Image: Yedoct, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

steps.tx: Workup follows the pattern rather than testing everything in every patient. Unilateral alternating attacks point toward **seronegative spondyloarthropathy**, so sacroiliac imaging and HLA-B27 testing help confirm the link. Bilateral granulomatous disease raises **sarcoidosis** with chest imaging and ACE, tuberculosis with Mantoux or interferon assay, syphilis serology and herpetic disease with raised pressure and iris atrophy. **Fuchs heterochromic iridocyclitis** shows heterochromia with stellate precipitates with cataract and glaucoma but without synechiae. Posner Schlossman crises cause recurrent pressure spikes with mild cells. Silent chronic bilateral disease in juvenile idiopathic arthritis needs screening.
steps.say: Workup is planned according to the pattern of attacks in anterior uveitis. Alternating attacks in a young adult with back stiffness suggest spondyloarthropathy, so HLA-B27 testing and sacroiliac imaging help the diagnosis. Bilateral granulomatous disease raises sarcoidosis, tuberculosis and syphilis, so chest imaging and blood tests guide the search. A pale iris with scattered stellate deposits and no adhesions suggests Fuchs disease. Children with arthritis need regular eye screening because their inflammation stays silent.

steps.tx: This chest film shows **bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy** with enlarged nodes on both sides in a patient worked up for granulomatous uveitis. Symmetric hilar enlargement is the classic pattern of **sarcoidosis**, which commonly pairs with bilateral granulomatous eye disease, raised ACE and skin or lung lesions. The film reminds students that eye inflammation can reveal systemic disease, so chest imaging belongs in bilateral granulomatous workup with tuberculosis tests and syphilis serology. Recognising this pattern earns marks and speeds referral.
steps.say: This chest film shows enlarged nodes sitting at both hila in a patient with granulomatous uveitis. Symmetric hilar enlargement strongly suggests sarcoidosis, which often causes bilateral eye inflammation with raised ACE. The image teaches an exam favourite that eye disease can uncover chest disease. Bilateral granulomatous uveitis therefore deserves chest imaging alongside tuberculosis and syphilis testing.

vis.alt: Chest radiograph showing bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy labeled as sarcoidosis workup for uveitis.
vis.caption: Bilateral hilar nodes on chest film in granulomatous uveitis workup Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: Treatment pairs intensive **topical steroids** with frequent prednisolone drops tapered by cell response and **cycloplegic mydriatics** with atropine or homatropine. Steroids quieten anterior chamber inflammation while mydriatics break and prevent posterior synechiae and relieve ciliary spasm pain. Raised pressure receives aqueous suppressants while herpetic disease adds oral antivirals. Severe bilateral recurrent or posterior involvement needs systemic steroids or immunosuppression with methotrexate, azathioprine or biologics. Dark glasses, rest and counselling support recovery while steroid induced pressure rise and cataract need monitoring.
steps.say: The standard pair for anterior uveitis combines steroid drops with dilating drops. Steroid drops calm the inflammation inside the front chamber and the dose falls as cells clear. Dilating drops stop the iris from sticking to the lens and they ease the aching spasm of the focusing muscle. Raised pressure receives pressure lowering treatment and herpetic cases add antiviral tablets. Severe or repeated disease needs tablets or injections that suppress immunity under specialist care.

steps.tx: Delayed treatment invites posterior synechiae with iris stuck to lens, irregular pupil, seclusio and angle closure, plus peripheral anterior synechiae, complicated cataract, **secondary glaucoma** from inflammation or steroids or synechial closure, cystoid macular oedema, hypotony with phthisis after ciliary shutdown and band keratopathy in chronic childhood disease. **Endophthalmitis** after surgery or trauma with pain, lid swelling, hypopyon and vitritis is the emergency mimic needing intravitreal antibiotics and vitrectomy rather than steroids alone. Penetrating injury also risks sympathetic ophthalmia in the fellow eye.
steps.say: Delay lets the iris glue itself to the lens and block the drain, so pressure rises and the pupil turns irregular. Chronic inflammation also clouds the lens, swells the macula and leaves calcium deposited on the cornea in children. Pus inside the eye after surgery or injury with pain and swelling means endophthalmitis, which needs antibiotic injections into the eye and often surgery. A penetrating injury also threatens the other eye with sympathetic inflammation, so urgent referral saves sight.
